analytic.title: Estimating Sonoran pronghorn abundance and survival with fecal DNA and capture-recapture methods

div.p: Population abundance estimates are important for management but can be challenging to determine in low-density, wide-ranging, and endangered species, such as Sonoran pronghorn (Antilocapra americana sonoriensis). The Sonoran pronghorn population has been increasing; however, population estimates are currently derived from a biennial aerial count that does not provide survival or recruitment estimates. We identified individuals through noninvasively collected fecal DNA and used robust-design capture-recapture to estimate abundance and survival for Sonoran pronghorn in the United States from 2013 to 2014. In 2014 we generated separate population estimates for pronghorn gathered near 13 different artificial water holes and for pronghorn not near water holes. The population using artificial water holes had 116 (95% CI 102-131) and 121 individuals (95% CI 112-132) in 2013 and 2014, respectively. For all locations, we estimated there were 144 individuals (95% CI 132-157). Adults had higher annual survival probabilities (0.83, 95% CI 0.69-0.92) than fawns (0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.65). Our use of targeted noninvasive genetic sampling and capture-recapture with Sonoran pronghorn fecal DNA was an effective method for monitoring a large proportion of the population. Our results provided the first survival estimates for this population in over 2 decades and precise estimates of the population using artificial water holes. Our method could be used for targeted sampling of broadly distributed species in other systems, such as in African savanna ecosystems, where many species congregate at watering sites.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Reliable population estimates are central to wildlife management and to determining species' conservation status and recovery success (IUCN 2012). However, obtaining reliable population estimates can be challenging, especially in low-density, wide-ranging species. Traditional methods of obtaining population estimates can require physical capture, which can be expensive and related to decreased fitness, a compromised immune system, impaired locomotion, and mortality (see Murray & Fuller 2000;Arnemo et al. 2006). Consequently, use of noninvasive sampling methods, such as track surveys, remote cameras, and collection of DNA samples to monitor wildlife has increased (Silviera et al. 2003;Waits & Paetkau 2005).

Fecal DNA microsatellite analysis is used to estimate population size, sex ratio, parentage, relatedness, and genetic structure (Waits & Paetkau 2005;Schwartz et al. 2007). Noninvasive genetic sampling and capturerecapture (NGS-CR) combination methods to estimate demographic parameters are well developed in carnivore monitoring (Prugh et al. 2005;Stansbury et al. 2014) and are being used increasingly with ungulates (e.g., Brinkman et al. 2011;Poole et al. 2011;Goode et al. 2014). Use of NGS-CR eliminates capture expense and capture-related stress on animals and provides accurate population estimates (e.g., DeBarba et al. 2010;Stansbury et al. 2014).

The Sonoran pronghorn (Antilocapra americana sonoriensis) occurs only in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona (U.S.A.) and Mexico and is endangered (USFWS 2015). By 2002 the U.S. population was approximately 21 individuals (USFWS 2015). To facilitate recovery efforts, a captive-breeding program was established on the Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge (CPNWR), and captive individuals are released annually into the wild (128 released since 2006 [USFWS 2015]). For the species to be downlisted or delisted, 6 criteria must be met, including a population size adequate to maintain a viable population over the long term (USFWS 2015). Abundance estimates are presently based on biennial aerial counts and sightability models to account for imperfect detection (USFWS 2015). The U.S. population estimate was 159 (95% CI 112-432) and 202 individuals (95% CI in December 2012and 2014, respectively (USFWS 2015). Although the current approach provides population estimates and trends, high costs prohibit annual population estimates, and the method does not provide information on survival, reproduction, or genetic diversity.

Pronghorn are sensitive to stress, and mortality from capture myopathy is not uncommon (Chalmers & Barrett 1977;Bright & Hervert 2005); thus, they are good candidates for NGS-CR monitoring. We sought to evaluate the feasibility of using NGS-CR to monitor pronghorn annual survival and population size. In 2013 and 2014, we designed and implemented a targeted sampling strategy for collecting fecal samples (Woodruff et al. 2015) during the hot, dry months (May-June) when Sonoran pronghorn congregate at artificial water sources (water holes).

Our first objective was to estimate annual survival probabilities for different sex and age classes. We expected to find higher annual survival probability for adults than fawns. Our second objective was to generate a population estimate and associated confidence interval for comparison with the current aerial estimate. Based on relocations of >100 radio-collared pronghorn from 2006 to 2013, approximately 30% of the population never visits an artificial water hole during summer (J. Hervert, personal communication), although the actual percentage is unknown. Thus, if our noninvasive methods were effective, we would expect an estimated population size approximately 30% lower than aerial counts.

div.head: Study Area
div.p: The study area encompassed approximately c 7000 km 2 on the CPNWR, Barry M. Goldwater Range (BMGR), and Organ Pipe National Monument (ORPI) (Fig. 1). Wide alluvial valleys divided by fault-block mountains characterize the region. Elevational range is 610-1219 m, but pronghorn are typically found below 900 m. Vegetation is sparse and consists primarily of mesquite (Prosopis velutina and P. glandulosa) shrublands and open hardwood, mixed cactus woodlands (Shreve & Wiggins 1964). Average annual precipitation is 7.5-20 cm (USFWS 2002) June and temperatures in the study area average over 38 °C in summer (INRMP 2003).

Natural surface water in the region is limited. Quitoboquito Spring, on ORPI, is the only naturally occurring year-round water source in current Sonoran pronghorn range (USFWS 2015). Motion-sensing cameras documented no pronghorn use at this spring during our study (University of Arizona data). Numerous artificial water holes provide supplemental water for pronghorn. From April through July, alfalfa hay is provided weekly for pronghorn at 6 artificial water holes.

div.head: Sample Collection
div.p: Sonoran pronghorn are distributed over approximately 11,000 km 2 (USFWS 2015), but low population density makes detection on the periphery of their range difficult. To increase efficiency, we implemented a targeted sampling approach (Puechmaille & Petit 2007;Rudnick et al. 2008;Stansbury et al. 2014). Radiotelemetry and aerial surveys show that Sonoran pronghorn use areas close to natural and artificial water sources more often than random locations (deVos & Miller 2005;Morgart et al. 2005), making targeted sampling at artificial water holes a practical method for sampling a majority of the population. In May-June 2013 and 2014, we collected fecal samples 3-4 times (6-7 total) at intervals of 7 d at all 17 artificial water holes likely to be used by pronghorn (Supporting Information), following the methods of Woodruff et al. (2015Woodruff et al. ( , 2015)). Sampling locations, frequencies, and intervals were limited by terrain, level of pronghorn use, logistical constraints to site access, and efforts to minimize pronghorn disturbance. Thus, we classified each sampling site as single-session or multisession. Based on 2013 results and weather conditions (i.e., wetter conditions and relatively better forage), we started 2014 sampling 12 d later than in 2013.

We collected samples within 50 m of water holes (Woodruff et al. 2015) and excluded feces piles that ap-peared to be from >1 individual based on pellet shape, color, and size. For each sampling event, we attempted to collect 3 times as many samples as the number of pronghorn counted at the water hole just prior to sampling (based on observation and motion-sensing cameras) to ensure sufficient recaptures (redetections) and maximize performance of capture-recapture estimators (Solberg et al. 2006). We placed at least 6 pellets from each feces pile in a small paper envelope and stored the envelopes at room temperature in a plastic bag with (ß250 mL) of silica desiccant (Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) to reduce DNA degradation. Remaining pellet groups were scattered outside the sampling area to avoid resampling them during a later visit.

We classified samples by freshness (F1, freshest [pellet visibly wet on outside]; F2, moderately fresh [pellet wet or moist on inside only, crushed easily]; F3, old [no moisture, crumbled when crushed]). We used a chi-square analysis test of independence (R version 3.1.2, www.rproject.org) to assess individual identification success by freshness and session (1-3).

In 2014, in an effort to also sample individuals not using artificial water holes, we targeted groups with radiocollared individuals located >1 km away from artificial water holes (hereafter, other sites) and opportunistically collected samples from 9 locations after observing defecation (Fig. 1).

div.head: Genetic Analyses
div.p: Methods of subsampling, DNA extraction, genotyping, genotyping error, and probability of identity calculations are described in Supporting Information.

div.head: Abundance and Survival Estimation
div.p: We classified fecal samples in the field through visual inspection of size and morphology as adult (ࣙ1 year old) or fawn (<1 year old). For 76% of individuals we cross-checked the age assignment against a fitted crossvalidation model developed from multiple pellet measurements (length, width, length to width ratio, volume) of individuals of known age (Woodruff et al. 2016).

Each sample for which DNA was successfully amplified was considered a detection. We generated an encounter history for each individual indicating detected (1) or not (0) in each sampling session, counting only a single detection per individual per sampling session. We collapsed sessions 3 and 4 into a single session because only 3 sites were sampled 4 times.

We applied Huggins' robust design in the development of 4 biologically appropriate models of survival and abundance (Table 3 & Supporting Information), which allowed varying survival and detection probabilities over time and variation in capture and recapture probability, (Pollock 1982;Huggins 1989;Pollock et al. 1990) in Program MARK (White & Burnham 1999). We used Huggins' models because our models included an individual covariate, and we believed we sampled a substantial proportion of the population. We assumed the population was demographically and geographically closed within the annual sampling occasions during which we estimated detection (p) and redetection (c) probabilities and abundance (N). Across years, gains (birth and immigration) and losses (death and emigration) in a population are expected, so we estimated annual apparent survival (ϕ). We modeled equal survival probability for male and female adults and varying survival probabilities by sex. We modeled the individual covariate fed or not fed on survival probability because supplemental feed was not provided at all sites.

Data from single and multisession sites were combined in the same model. Although redetection of individuals from single-session artificial-water-hole sites was possible at multisession artificial water holes and vice versa, we never detected the same individual at both single and multisession artificial water holes within the same year. We hypothesized that visitation to artificial water holes differs by sex and estimated detection and redetection probabilities and abundance in groups (males and females at both single-session and multisession sites), resulting in 4 estimates. To evaluate differences between sessions in a single year, we modeled time-varying detection probabilities and redetection probabilities. To estimate detection probability at single-session sites, we used the modelestimated mean detection probability from multisession sites by sex (i.e., mean male-detection probability at multisession sites equaled detection probability for males at single-session sites). We used means coding in the design matrix to estimate mean detection probability by sex. Before fitting models, parameter estimates for single-session redetection probabilities were fixed at zero and emigration parameters (δ) were also fixed to zero due to lack of precision (Lukacs et al. 2009). Because we expanded our sampling extent in 2014, we performed analyses on artificial-water-hole locations in 2013 and 2014, and on all locations (i.e., including other sites) in 2014.

We used separate closed-capture models in each year to estimate fawn detection and redetection probabilities and abundance in 2013 and 2014, again, modeling artificial water holes sites only and all locations separately. We used a full-likelihood robust design model to estimate annual apparent survival for the 2013 fawn cohort. We included models with and without time variation of detection and redetection probabilities. We estimated fawn survival from approximately 3 to 15 months of age. Survival in neonates is highly stochastic, and analysis of survival in older fawns may be more sensitive to current environmental conditions or management practices and provide a more meaningful indicator of current population growth.

All adult and fawn models assumed equal detection and redetection probability (i.e., no behavioral effect) because it is unlikely that the initial detection would affect subsequent detections. We did not detect fawns at single-session sites in 2013. However, in 2014 we did and used the model-estimated mean fawn detection probability at multisession sites for single-session sites. We used Akaike's information criterion (AIC c ) corrected for small sample size to evaluate relative support for each model. We model averaged parameter estimates and standard errors over all models (Burnham & Anderson 2002). We summed population estimates for each group (6 groups: single and multisession for each of adult male, adult female, and fawn) and calculated standard errors for abundance with the Delta method (Seber 1982).

div.head: Sample Collection and Genetic Analysis
div.p: From 13 sites with artificial water holes, we collected 730 samples in 2013 and 980 samples in 2014 and extracted 634 and 692 samples in 2013 and 2014 (Table 1). We also collected and extracted 79 samples from 9 other sites in 2014 (Supporting Information). Four single-session artificial-water-hole sites had no indication of recent pronghorn use.

In 2013 and 2014, 75% (n = 474) and 72% (n = 555), respectively, of samples achieved a consensus genotype for individual identification. Allelic dropout rates were higher than false alleles, and overall genotyping error rates were slightly higher in 2014 (Table 1). Our final data set contained no individuals that were mismatched at only 1 locus and 1 pair of samples that were mismatched at 2 out of 10 loci. We amplified these samples at an additional 6 loci and found 4 mismatches at the 16 loci, and the samples were determined to be from 2 individuals.

div.head: Abundance and Survival Estimation
div.p: We had 474 detections of 91 individuals (50 adult males, 24 adult females, 17 fawns) in 2013 and 555 detections of 127 individuals (69 adult males, 38 adult females, 20 fawns) in 2014. Twenty-one of the individuals (8 adult males, 10 adult females, 3 fawns) in 2014 were detected at 9 other sites (i.e., non artificial water holes), 4 of which were also detected at artificial water holes (Table 2). Sixty-three individuals detected in 2013 were also detected in 2014. The number of detections per individual (i.e., samples) in a year ranged from 1 to 32, and 33.7% and 26.0% were single detections in 2013 and 2014, respectively. At artificial water holes we detected 2.5-3 times more adult male than female samples, and the average number of detections per individual was 6.1 and 3.6 for adult males and females, respectively.

For artificial-water-holes sites only and all sites, the top model was the same and included equal survival (ϕ) by sex and equal detection and redetection probabilities, both varying by time and group (Table 3 & Supporting Information). Males had higher detection probabilities (mean 0.68, 95% CI 0.55-0.77) than females (mean 0.47, 95% CI 0.31-0.63) in all sampling occasions across years. In 2013 detection probabilities were highest in session 3. They increased from 0.66 in session 1 to 0.76 in session 3 for males and from 0.37 to 0.49 for females. Detection probabilities were highest for both males and females in session 1 in 2014 and remained relatively constant over time. Annual apparent adult survival probability was 0.83 (95% CI 0.69-0.92).

Across years for artificial-water-holes sites only and all locations, the top model for abundance estimation of fawns included equal detection and redetection probabilities and time variation (Table 3 & Supporting Information). Consistent with adults, fawn-detection probabilities were highest in session 3 in year 1 and in session 1 in year 2 (mean 0.48, 95% CI 0.25-0.70). The best AIC c model for fawn survival had constant and equal detection and redetection probabilities (Table 3 & Supporting Information). The second best model differed only in that detection and redetection probabilities varied over time. As expected, fawn survival probability was lower than adult survival at 0.41 (95% CI 0.21-0.65).

At artificial-water-hole sites, the models produced (summed) population estimates of 116 individuals (95% CI 101-132) in 2013 and 121 individuals (95% CI 112-132) in 2014. For all locations (2014 only), the estimate was 144 individuals (95% CI 132-157). Estimates indicated a bias toward males; there were 1.4-1.6 times more adult males than adult females. When comparing annual estimates from sites with artificial water holes, the results suggest little to no change in population size.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Our new method of using NGS-CR with Sonoran pronghorn fecal DNA provided the first survival estimates in over 20 years and precise estimates of the population using artificial water holes. Targeted sampling allowed collection of many pellet groups, and high detection probabilities resulted in high precision (Burnham et al. 1987). Capture-recapture analysis assumes all individuals in a population have equal capture probability (Link 2004;Lukacs & Burnham 2005), yet individual heterogeneity is inherent in capture probability due to differences in sex and age class, dominance, or individual location in relation to the trap (Ebert et al. 2010). Although our estimates were precise, they are likely biased low because they represent only the portion of the population using artificial water holes.

div.head: Genetic Analyses
div.p: Although we had moderate to high genotyping errors (average allelic dropout rate 12.1%, average false allele rate 3.4), we are confident this did not result in misidentification because after conducting 3-8 replicates per sample and correcting for errors, all samples had ࣘ3 mismatches. Individual identification success rates were lower and genotyping error rates were higher in 2014 than in 2013, but we could not identify any field protocols or environmental conditions that changed. One possible explanation is a change in extraction chemistry from 2013 to 2014. All samples were extracted using the Qiagen QIAamp DNA stool mini kit (Qiagen Inc., Valencia, CA, USA), but Qiagen changed the composition of the kits in 2014 from an InhibitEX tablet to a liquid InhibitEX buffer.

In both years, samples from 2 sites (Devil Hills and Point of Pintas) made up approximately 50% of failed samples and 47% and 28% of samples with genotyping errors in 2013 and 2014, respectively. These sites were on the typically hotter western side of the BMGR. Site-wide maximum daily temperatures were 33.6-44.4 °C, and daily maximum temperatures in western BMGR during sampling averaged 2.5 °C higher than in eastern locations. Increased UV radiation and high temperatures elevate the rate of DNA degradation (Murphy et al. 2007;DeMay et al. 2013), which may explain the lower success rates at western sites. Decreasing the length of time between sampling occasions would allow for collection of fresher pellets and reduce pellet exposure to environmental conditions (Woodruff et al. 2015) but would increase effort and pronghorn disturbance.

div.head: Abundance and Survival Estimation
div.p: The large spatial range and low-density of Sonoran pronghorn limited us to a targeted sampling design conducted during the hot, dry months to maximize detection probability. Year-to-date rainfall when we began sampling was higher in 2013 (3.4 cm) than in 2014 (1.1 cm). Weather and range conditions likely play a substantial role in detection probabilities because visitation to artificial water holes declined under cooler, wetter conditions when there was adequate natural forage. To account for the increasing probability of detection and the identification of more individuals in later sessions in 2013 (51 and 77 individuals in the sessions 1 and 3, respectively), we began sampling 12 d later in 2014. In contrast, detection probabilities were highest in session 1 in 2014, and we identified 83 and 76 individuals in sessions 1 and 3, respectively. We suspect when we initiated sampling in 2013 use of artificial water holes was not at the maximum. Our inconsistent detection probabilities across sessions also provide an explanation for why the best models included time variation.

Detection probabilities were substantially higher in our study (0.36-0.76) relative to other ungulate studies (range 0.01-0.38 [Poole et al. 2011;Ebert et al. 2012a, Conservation Biology Volume 30, No. 5, 2016 2012b; Goode et al. 2014]) and were noticeably higher (1.45 times) in males than in females. Contrary to similar ungulate studies (Poole et al. 2011;Ebert et al. 2012aEbert et al. , 2012b)), we detected twice as many adult males as adult females at artificial water holes (male:female ratios of 2.1:1). We detected approximately the same numbers of males and females at other sites and ratios were 1.8:1 in 2014 when we included other sites. The higher number of males (ratio: 1.4:1-1.6:1) was unexpected. Prior to the 2003 population crash, females constituted approximately 60% of the population (Wright & deVos 1986;Hughes & Smith 1990), and 2014 telemetry flight data indicated male:female ratios were approximately 0.66:1 (J. Hervert, personal communication).

Due to our targeted sampling design, inferences based on our estimates apply largely to the individuals using artificial water holes. Twice as many captive-bred males have been released as females, which may lead to more males using artificial water holes. Released animals may use artificial water holes more readily because they are conditioned to provision of food and water (US-FWS 2015). Home range size and movement rates likely differ between sexes (Ockenfels et al. 1994;Clemente et al. 1995), which could affect the use and representation of the sexes at artificial water holes. These factors may have contributed to our greater detection of males in the population. In the future, extrapolation to the entire population, especially pertaining to male:female ratios, would need to include a sex-ratio correction factor.

Male pronghorn may also defecate more frequently than female pronghorn. Male duikers (Sylvicapra grimmia) defecate more frequently for marking territory (Lunt et al. 2007;Lunt & Mhlanga 2011), and dominant male oribi (Ourebia ourebi) limit defecation to increase territory-marking frequency (Brashares & Arcese 1999a,1999b). However, Irby (1981) determined no significant differences in defecation rates between sexes of American pronghorn (Antilocapra americana). Further work is needed to determine whether defecation rates vary between sexes around artificial water holes.

Detection probability for fawns was generally lower than for adults, and fawns had 4 of the 6 lowest detection probabilities. Nonetheless, the highest detection probability (0.79) was for fawns in session 1 of 2014, which also had the highest detection probability for adult females (0.57). Detection probability of fawns is correlated with that of adult females likely because young were traveling with their mothers. Typically, NGS-CR studies delineate sex with no analysis of detection probability or abundance by age, unless additional data is collected from cameras or physical capture. Our method allowed determination of an individual's age from fecal pellet measurements (Woodruff et al. 2016), which provided fine-scale delineation of demographic parameters.

Age class best explained survival probability; fawns had much lower survival probabilities than adults. Ungulate survival is generally lowest in the first year (Zager & White 2003;DelGiudice et al. 2006), and survival can be <10% for neonates ࣘ4 months of age (Franzmann et al. 1980;Ballard et al. 1991;Zager & White 2003). Fawns had low survival probability (0.41), although 2013 had the highest recruitment documented since the population crash (J. Hervert, personal communication). Although our survival estimates represent only a single year of survival probabilities, they provide a baseline for continuing monitoring of survival trends. They are also the first survival estimates since the 1980s when mean adult survival was estimated at 0.93 during a period of aboveaverage rainfall (deVos & Miller 2005). A 1996 population viability analysis (PVA) indicated probability of persistence for this population was strongly affected by adult survival but suggested fawn survival was perhaps even more significant (Hosack et al. 2002), although a more recent PVA indicates precipitation was the most important factor in population persistence (Horne et al. 2016). Fawn survival is innately tied to precipitation (Bright & Hervert 2005), and total rainfall in 2013 (approximately 25 cm) was the highest in the past decade (average 19 cm, range 6-25 cm annually, http:// http://www.earthonly.com/ajo/weather/).

Given our high detection probabilities, our survival estimate is likely unbiased, yet the precision (CI 0.69-0.92) is low due to our small sample size. Adult survival probabilities in this population did not differ by sex. Although exceptions exist (Van Vuren & Bray 1986;Fancy et al. 1994;Toïgo et al. 1997), adult survival probability of male ungulates is generally lower than females (Gaillard et al. 1993;Owen-Smith 1993;Loison et al. 1999), particularly in polygynous species, due to competition for breeding opportunities (see Clutton-Brock & Isvaran 2007). However, Loisin et al. (1999) suggest when food resources are abundant, there may not be sex differences in survival. Although food resources in this population are not abundant, the provision of supplemental food and water before breeding season, when resources are the most limited, may mitigate differences in adult survival probabilities.

Population estimates at sites with artificial water holes were 60% (121, 95% CI 112-132) of the December 2014 aerial count (202,. However, our upper CI was 77% of the lower CI from the aerial count. Our minimum count was 110 individuals at artificial water holes relative to 168 individuals from the aerial survey. The difference in population estimates likely arises from a lower detection probability in the aerial survey. The trade-off in the wider geographic sampling of the aerial survey is lower precision in both detection probability and population estimation. Our results indicate that a substantial portion of the population is sampled by targeted sampling at artificial water holes and could be useful for determining population trends. Captive-bred collared animals continue to be released into the population annually, and the ratio of collared animals to uncollared animals at artificial and other sites could be used to adjust estimates of population trend determined by NGS-CR.

div.head: Management Implications
div.p: Sonoran pronghorn in the United States are geographically and genetically distinct from other pronghorn in North America. The long-term persistence of the population continues to be tenuous (USFWS 2015). Although NGS-CR methods are less common for population estimation of ungulates, our results indicate this method is useful for Sonoran pronghorn. Genotyping for individual identification provides minimum counts and the ability to incorporate capture-recapture methods for precise demographic estimates. As the population continues to expand, this method should allow managers to monitor trends in abundance and survival as an indicator of the population's trajectory, as opposed to aerial survey methods, which provide abundance estimates but are costly and do not provide information on survival or other demographic parameters. Combining NGS-CR data with information garnered from radio-collared individuals, such as mortality and movement data, would greatly improve the understanding of the population's viability. This method also presents opportunities for targeted sampling in other systems for broadly distributed species, such as in African savanna ecosystems, where animals congregate at watering sites in the dry season (Cain et al. 2012).
